vignette:
Marisol is a 37-year-old hotel manager who came to treatment months after a sexual assault by a male guest she had interacted with during a late shift. She can describe pieces of that night with painful clarity-the smell of his cologne in the corridor, the patterned carpet outside the room, the moment he stepped too close-but when she tries to put the whole event into words, her speech stalls. She says she knows what happened, yet "the story won't come out right," and in session she circles fragments, falls silent, and looks down in visible shame. What has stayed with her most forcefully is not a coherent sequence but a felt collapse into humiliation. Even remembering it in flashes leaves her flushed and rigid, as if her own body were exposing her.

In the weeks afterward, Marisol had come to believe that the assault said something final about her. She was certain there was something defective in her, some flaw in her character that had made her the kind of woman this could happen to. When her heart raced or her stomach dropped unexpectedly, she did not read those reactions as ordinary fear responses but as proof that her body had become an enemy, still acting as if danger were present. Those beliefs colored the way she remembered the assault. Each attempt to think it through became less like recalling an event and more like confronting evidence against herself; the memory collapsed into shame, and the more ashamed she felt, the harder it was to find words or make a clear story even in her own mind.

Those same beliefs began to shape what she did every day. Working in a hotel meant constant exposure to men who resembled the guest in age, build, grooming, or manner, and Marisol started reorganizing her routines to avoid them whenever she could. She would ask a supervisor to handle a complaint from a certain type of guest, linger in the back office rather than cross the lobby, or choose service corridors over the main hall if a man with similar cologne or a similar haircut was at the front desk. She also began staying later and later at work, telling herself she was being responsible, but privately knowing that if she kept moving-checking occupancy, covering desk problems, answering late emails-she could postpone being alone with her thoughts. At home, when she could no longer distract herself, she turned things over endlessly in her mind, rehearsing fantasies of revenge against the man who assaulted her. In those hours she felt driven to imagine how to get even, as though this mental vigilance might undo what had happened or restore something damaged in her.

Yet these strategies tightened the problem. Because Marisol spent so much energy avoiding men who looked like him and filling every spare hour with work, she rarely let herself approach the memory long enough for it to become more organized. When it did break through, it arrived in the same jagged pieces, stripped of context and soaked in shame. The revenge rumination also kept her fixed on the assault in a hot, repetitive way without helping her describe it; she would replay single moments and imagined confrontations, but the larger narrative stayed inaccessible. Each failure to tell a coherent story seemed to confirm her worst conclusions: that there was something wrong with her, that even her own mind and body were not functioning as they should.

Over time, that loop spread into her relationship and her work life. Her partner noticed that she was rarely home before late evening and that when she was home, she seemed far away, mentally preoccupied and tense. Marisol offered practical explanations-staff shortages, guest issues, end-of-quarter demands-but inside she was avoiding the quiet in which the memory might surface. At work she remained competent, even excessively so, but colleagues began to comment on how she never seemed to switch off. The cost of that overcontrol became most obvious on days when a guest's voice, cologne, or physical resemblance caught her off guard. She would feel her body react instantly, and that reaction would feed her conviction that she was permanently changed in some damaged way. Then she would work harder, avoid more, and later find herself again trapped in bitter, wordless replay.

By the time she sought help, Marisol was exhausted by how narrow her life had become. What finally brought her in was not one dramatic crisis but the realization that she could manage an entire hotel more easily than she could sit alone for ten minutes without being pulled into shame or revenge fantasies. She is frightened that if she ever stops controlling her schedule and her surroundings, the memory will overwhelm her completely. At the same time, she hopes-carefully, almost reluctantly-that she might be able to tell what happened in words, and that doing so might loosen her certainty that the assault revealed something rotten about who she is.
